design_detail: Methodological essay (journal section 'Perspectives', Archives of General Psychiatry, 5 printed pages, 35 references; two authors, both PhD; supported in part by a National Institute of Mental Health grant). It argues that clinicians and researchers disagree about the long-term course of conditions such as schizophrenia, alcoholism and opiate addiction (the paper's terms) partly because they see different samples: a clinician sees the people ill at a given moment (a prevalence or census sample), in which each person's chance of being present is proportional to how long the illness lasts, whereas follow-up research comes closer to everyone who ever develops the condition (an incidence sample). The mechanism is shown with an invented, skewed distribution of illness duration in seven intervals (Fig. 1) reweighted by duration into the sample met on ward rounds (Fig. 2), a variant with a six-month duration requirement, and an approximate illustration from New York State mental health facilities. Other selection biases of clinical samples are described in prose (recovery without treatment, longer illness before treatment, an apparent link between early onset and poor outcome, Berkson's bias, selection on symptoms distorting correlations), followed by recommendations for research reports. No new data; the empirical examples are cited from other authors, and the authors state twice that they do not present or evaluate empirical evidence (pp. 1179, 1180). Filed as modelling: the evidence is a worked numerical illustration of a sampling mechanism, not a test against data.
can_establish: That, by arithmetic, a sample of the people ill at one moment over-represents long-lasting cases whenever durations vary widely relative to their mean, so that the course seen in clinics can look far worse than the course of everyone who develops the condition; and which reporting (duration of illness, prior episodes, how people were selected) lets readers judge this.
cannot_establish: How large the distortion is for any real condition or treatment population, including people treated for opioid or alcohol problems (no real duration distribution is analysed and the New York figures are approximate and unsourced), or the recovery rates it quotes from other studies, which it neither reproduces nor appraises.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (no participants). The model uses an invented distribution of illness duration in seven intervals with means of 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 months (Fig. 1, p. 1179). The real-world illustration uses approximate counts for facilities sponsored or licensed by the New York State Office of Mental Health in New York City, with no source or year (p. 1181). Empirical examples are cited from other authors: references 5–9 on the outcome of alcohol problems, references 11–15 on schizophrenia, Schacter (1982) on smoking and obesity (p. 1178), and Robins (1974) and Robins, Helzer, Hesselbrock and Wish (1980) on Vietnam veterans (p. 1179).
sample.selection_effects: The examples were chosen by the authors to show clinical pessimism contradicted by research; no search or criteria are stated. The paper itself names a 1982 dispute over a controlled-drinking study (reference 1) as its example of a disputed prognosis for alcoholism (p. 1178), and it does not appraise the recovery figures it quotes.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. In the model the quantity that matters is the length of each person's illness, which sets the chance of being seen in a clinic on a given day.

comparison.controls: The model compares the duration distribution of everyone who develops the illness (Fig. 1) with that of the people present on one day in a clinic that treats every case for its whole duration (Fig. 2, p. 1179); the New York illustration compares a one-day census of treated patients with a year's period prevalence and with a year's intakes (p. 1181).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (no data). The argument concerns this problem: in a prevalence sample compared with controls, characteristics that make an illness last longer cannot be told apart from characteristics that cause it (p. 1181).

outcomes.instruments: Arithmetic of duration-weighted sampling: each interval's share of the population multiplied by its mean duration and renormalized (the products sum to 1,068, Fig. 1 legend, p. 1179); mean durations of the population and of the clinic-day sample; the same after excluding cases ill less than six months (p. 1180).
outcomes.validity_norms: No comparison with an observed clinic sample. The authors state that the distortion depends not on the shape of the distribution but only on how variable duration is relative to its mean (pp. 1179–1180), and refer to Freeman and Hutchison (1980) for estimating the population distribution from durations to date (p. 1180).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Clinician's illusion': attributing the characteristics and course of the people currently ill to everyone who develops the illness, which in epidemiological terms is using a prevalence sample as a substitute for an incidence sample (p. 1180).

analysis.effect_sizes: Not applicable (no estimates). Model quantities, all reproducible from Fig. 1 (editors' check: interval shares of 40, 25, 15, 10, 5, 3 and 2% reproduce the printed sum of 1,068 and every value below): population mean duration 10.7 months, median under six months, one tenth lasting more than two years; clinic-day sample mean 50.8 months; the longest-lasting 2% of the population make up nearly a quarter of the clinic sample (editors' calculation 24.0%) and the shortest-lasting 40% make up 7.5%; each person in the longest interval is 64 times as likely to be met as each person in the shortest, or 128 times if also twice as likely to be in treatment; after excluding cases under six months, 35% of the population remain, with a mean of 25.4 months and a clinic-sample mean of 60.5 months (pp. 1179–1180). New York illustration, called approximate by the authors: about 15,000 patients in treatment at any moment and about 15,000 admissions a year; in a one-day census about 95% have been hospitalized more than a year (average more than 20 years) and at least 60% will still be there two years later; a year's period prevalence of about 29,250; intakes have a median stay of about three weeks; the census and a year's intakes overlap by about 5% (p. 1181).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable. The recovery figures quoted from other studies are given without definitions, denominators or appraisal.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A worked hypothetical example showing that, when illness durations vary widely, the people in treatment on a given day are dominated by long-lasting cases (mean 50.8 against 10.7 months in the invented population), qualitative descriptions of other selection biases in clinical samples, and an approximate New York illustration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The introduction presents the mechanism as a neglected problem that could account wholly or in large measure for the disagreement between clinicians and researchers about prognosis (p. 1178), while the authors state that they intend no substantive conclusions (p. 1179) and do not present or evaluate empirical evidence (p. 1180); the mechanism is shown to be possible, not shown to explain any particular disagreement. The recovery figures for alcohol problems, Vietnam veterans and smoking are presented as findings that 'forcefully contradicted' clinical views (p. 1179) without definitions or appraisal. The Comment recommends caution when advising lay people on the natural history of chronic illnesses (p. 1182).

timeline.event: Berkson describes how hospital samples can show associations between conditions that are unrelated in the population (Berkson, 1946, as cited by Cohen & Cohen, p. 1180).
Robins' Special Action Office monograph on Vietnam veterans, cited together with Robins, Helzer, Hesselbrock and Wish (1980) as the source of the 71% and 88% figures (references 17 and 18, p. 1179).
Robins, Helzer and Davis (1975), an interview study of 898 Vietnam returnees, is on file (card sc_robins_1975); this reader did not check whether it contains the figures Cohen and Cohen quote.
Freeman and Hutchison on estimating incidence and duration from prevalence samples (as cited, p. 1180).
Schacter: more than 60% of once-heavy smokers who tried to quit no longer smoked (as cited, p. 1178).
Robins (1993), 'Vietnam veterans' rapid recovery from heroin addiction: A fluke or normal expectation?', on file and read by another first reader in this round.
Heyman (2013), 'Quitting drugs: Quantitative and qualitative features', on file and read by another first reader in this round.

replication.where_it_stands: The sampling mechanism is arithmetic and reproducible; what it implies for any drug depends on real duration data, which the essay does not provide. Figures on recovery from opioid or alcohol problems should come from the primary studies on file (Robins et al., 1975; Robins, 1993; Heyman, 2013), not from this essay. For the site's 'Seven questions': the essay supports question 1 (people in treatment are not everyone who uses a drug, and on a given day over-represent those whose problems last longest), bears on question 2 and on 'linked to is not causes' (prevalence samples cannot separate what prolongs a problem from what causes it; Berkson's bias can create associations in treated groups), and says nothing about doses (3), significance (4), absolute numbers (5), replication (6) or headlines (7).

funding.funder: Supported in part by grant MH 36971 from the National Institute of Mental Health (p. 1182).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Patricia Cohen: New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University School of Public Health; Jacob Cohen: New York University (p. 1178). One of the five schizophrenia follow-up studies cited for a favourable natural history (reference 14) lists P. Cohen among its authors (p. 1182). Recorded as a flag, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For a given drug problem, following everyone who develops it in a defined community (an incidence cohort, treated or not) and comparing their course with that of a one-day census of people in treatment drawn from the same population, with the duration of problem use recorded for both.

domains.domain: Model assumptions and their empirical support
domains.note: The duration distribution is invented; the authors say its skewed shape may suit some illnesses but not others and that the distortion depends only on the variability of duration relative to its mean (pp. 1179–1180). A constant chance of treatment over the illness is assumed; departures are discussed in words (p. 1180).

domains.domain: Comparison with the phenomenon it explains
domains.note: No real clinic or population sample is analysed; the New York figures are approximate and unsourced (p. 1181); the disputed prognoses are cited, not shown to arise from this mechanism.
Every model value can be recomputed from Fig. 1 and its legend; the editors re-derived 10.7, 50.8, 25.4 and 60.5 months.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.note: The cited evidence is by others; one cited schizophrenia follow-up (reference 14) is co-authored by P. Cohen.
The authors state that they draw no substantive conclusions and present or evaluate no empirical evidence (pp. 1179, 1180).

domains.domain: Balance (examples in which clinical samples and population studies agree are not given)
domains.note: Every example shows clinicians more pessimistic than research. The paper concedes that studies of clinical samples are useful when their conclusions are limited to people seen in similar services (p. 1181) and notes that the alcohol findings were disputed (p. 1178), but does not appraise the recovery figures it relies on.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a methodological essay built on a hypothetical model (METHODS §5.3); the domains follow the editors' modelling cards (for example sc_bressloff_2001) and narrative-review checklist. The overall 'high' reflects only that the model is never tested against data, under the rule that the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Cite the essay for the mechanism (people in treatment on a given day over-represent long-lasting cases, with the consequences the authors list) and for its reporting recommendations, labelling its numbers as a hypothetical illustration; do not cite it for the size of the effect in any real population or for the recovery figures it quotes, which need their primary sources.

key_findings.finding: Mechanism: a clinician who sees the people ill on a given day meets each person with a probability proportional to how long that person's illness lasts, so a current (prevalence or census) sample over-represents long-lasting cases compared with everyone who ever develops the illness (an incidence sample); the authors call attributing the course of current patients to everyone who develops the illness the clinician's illusion.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1178); opening section (no heading), 12th–13th paragraphs (p. 1179) and 18th paragraph, 'In sum' (p. 1180)
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 1 ('Who was studied?'). The argument is about people met in treatment; prisons are not mentioned.

key_findings.finding: Hypothetical example: in an invented population whose illness lasts a mean of 10.7 months (median under six months; one tenth longer than two years), the people present in a clinic on a given day have a mean duration of 50.8 months, more than four years, and the longest-lasting 2% of the population make up nearly a quarter of that clinic sample.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 and its legend, Fig. 2 (p. 1179); opening section, 11th paragraph (p. 1179) and 13th paragraph (p. 1179, continuing on p. 1180)
key_findings.note: Numbers chosen by the authors to illustrate. Editors' check: interval shares of 40, 25, 15, 10, 5, 3 and 2% (40, 25 and 2% are printed; the others are read from Fig. 1) reproduce the printed sum of 1,068, both means and a 24.0% share for the longest-lasting 2%.

key_findings.finding: Each person in the longest-lasting group (mean 128 months) is 64 times as likely to be met on a given day as each person in the shortest-lasting group (mean 2 months), and 128 times if the longest-lasting are also twice as likely to be in treatment; the bias grows when treatment is most likely for long-lasting cases, which the authors think is probably the more frequent pattern in real clinics.

Requiring six months of illness for the diagnosis does not remove the distortion: in the example the remaining 35% of the population have a mean duration of 25.4 months, and a clinic sample of them 60.5 months.

Further biases of treatment samples, described without data: people who recover without entering treatment tend to have a better outlook; people entering treatment have usually been ill longer; the apparent link between early onset and poor outcome can be an artefact, because people with early onset who recovered are no longer there to be seen; people with a second, unrelated condition are more likely to be in treatment (Berkson's fallacy), so conditions unrelated in the population can appear together in a clinic (their example: depression with alcohol problems); and selecting people on either of two positively correlated characteristics can make their correlation negative in the sample.
key_findings.locator: Other Sources of Bias in Samples From Clinical Settings, 2nd–6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 1 and on 'linked to is not causes': associations seen among people in treatment can be produced by who enters treatment.

key_findings.finding: In a prevalence sample compared with controls there is likely to be no way to separate characteristics that affect how long an illness lasts from characteristics that cause it; the authors distinguish this from the more familiar problem that prevalence samples cannot separate causes of a disease from its consequences.
key_findings.locator: The Clinician's Illusion and Disparities Among Research Findings, 5th–6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 2 ('Were they tested before they started?'): the point concerns who remains ill, not a measurement before first use.

key_findings.finding: Approximate New York illustration: about 15,000 patients are in facilities sponsored or licensed by the New York State Office of Mental Health at any moment, with about 15,000 admissions a year; in a one-day census about 95% have been hospitalized more than a year (average more than 20 years) and at least 60% will still be there two years later, whereas for intakes the median duration may be about three weeks, with only a tiny proportion still in treatment two years later; the one-day census and a year's intakes overlap by only about 5%.
key_findings.locator: The Clinician's Illusion and Disparities Among Research Findings, 9th–10th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The authors call these figures approximate and dependent on the treatment system; no source or year is given.

key_findings.finding: Recovery figures quoted from other studies: at least half of people with serious alcohol problems recover completely, many without formal treatment (references 5–9, as summarized); more than 60% of once-heavy smokers who tried to quit no longer smoked (Schacter, 1982); of Vietnam veterans addicted to heroin when interviewed after returning to the United States, 71% were drug free two and a half years later, often without great effort, and of all who became addicted in Vietnam 88% avoided relapse over the three years after return (Robins, 1974; Robins et al., 1980).
key_findings.locator: Opening section, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 1178) and 6th paragraph (p. 1179); references 16–18 (p. 1182)
key_findings.note: Second-hand: no definitions ('addicted', 'drug free', 'relapse'), denominators or methods are given, and the two Vietnam figures are cited to two sources together. Anchor any figure in the primary studies (robins_1975 and robins_1993 are on file).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that they draw no substantive conclusions and do not present or evaluate empirical evidence on any issue; the essay only illustrates problems that arise when findings are interpreted incautiously.
key_findings.locator: Opening section, 7th paragraph (p. 1179); Other Sources of Bias, 4th paragraph (p. 1180)

key_findings.finding: The same mechanism produces disagreement among research findings: studies of people attending a service are often taken to represent everyone with the disorder, which is justified only when conclusions are limited to people seen in similar services; even first admissions vary widely in prior illness (psychotic symptoms for under a week to over five years before a first admission, as cited); a cited review of 30 years of medical research articles found the data needed to describe samples increasingly absent; and without a careful account of treatment history and selection the population to which findings apply is unknown, for which the authors judge the reporting standards of the time inadequate.
key_findings.locator: The Clinician's Illusion and Disparities Among Research Findings, 1st–3rd and 11th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 1, and on question 7 in the sense that a finding from a treated sample says nothing about everyone unless the selection is described.

key_findings.finding: Factors that maximize the distortion: variance of duration large relative to its mean; fluctuating, episodic symptoms with sporadic treatment by several services, so that recovered patients do not return while relapsed patients do; unclear onset and history; treatment that reduces symptoms rather than curing; and specialists who do not meet recovered patients in other settings.
key_findings.locator: Factors Relating to the Magnitude of the Clinician's Illusion, items 1–5
key_findings.note: The paper does not apply these factors to any drug treatment service.

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: report the duration of illness and the number of prior episodes in studies of clinical populations; consider studying new cases rather than all current cases (with the risk of recruiting too few); take prior duration into account whenever the course of illness is studied; treat natural-history studies of cases unselected for duration (and preferably for treatment) as crucial; and be cautious in advising lay people about the natural history of chronic illnesses.

reporting_issues.issue: The invented population distribution is given only as a bar chart: the text states the shares of three of the seven intervals (40%, 25% and 2%), and the other four must be read from Fig. 1; they are recoverable only because the legend prints the weighted sum of 1,068.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the illustration is reproducible, but a claim giving the clinic-sample share of the longest-lasting group should use the text's 'nearly a quarter', or the editors' 24.0% labelled as a calculation.

reporting_issues.issue: The two Vietnam figures (71% drug free two and a half years later; 88% avoiding relapse over three years) are cited to two sources together (references 17 and 18) without saying which figure comes from which, and without definitions or denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures cannot be checked from this paper; the card for Robins (1993) in this round and the existing card sc_robins_1975 are the places to anchor them.

reporting_issues.issue: The New York census and intake figures, including the 5% overlap, are given without a source or year.
reporting_issues.consequence: Usable only as the authors' approximate illustration, not as data.
